fields.meaning: May…, there is a risk that…
examples: If there had been a lot of people, it was a situation that could have turned into a major accident.
If we just carry on doing nothing like this, we could well be called irresponsible.
Normally nobody would do something like that, but he just might.
If it isn't repaired properly, it could lead to an accident.
In this recession, even our company could end up in the red.
My husband is so busy with work that he is at risk of dying from overwork.
fields.explain:
Placed after Vます to predict a bad consequence: ～Vます＋ かねない .
Formal style, leaning toward written language/speeches/reports.
Often used with risk-related vocabulary:誤解を招く,問題になる,批判される,破綻する,失う,危険だ.
Not used for the speaker's own volition or own future plans.
Not used for positive results (avoid:成功し かねない ), unless the sentence is ironic.

• Expresses a risk or high possibility of something happening (usually a bad, undesirable result) based on the speaker's judgment.
• Nuance of warning/reminder: “It could lead to…, you know”. It does not mean “cannot” like ～かねる.
• More subjective than おそれがある; it involves evaluation and consideration of the situation.
• Often used in analyses, news and reports: “～しかねない”, “～になりかねない”.
• Not used to talk about one's own ability (it does not mean “can/cannot do”).
fields.notes:
• Common phrases: ～になりかねない, ～を招きかねない, ～を失いかねない, ～に見られかねない (could easily be seen as…).
• Often combined with つい, このままでは, 安易に, 軽率な, 不適切な to emphasize the risk.
• The past form is rare (～かねなかった) and sounds stiff; the present ～かねない is preferred for general statements.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～かねる (cannot do) — the two patterns have opposite meanings and very different pragmatics.
Using it for positive results: wrong nuance. Avoid “この案は成功しかねない”.
Using it for purely objective possibility: choose おそれがある or うる instead.
Subject “I” with the speaker's own volition/action: inappropriate (the pattern evaluates consequences).

examples: I'm very sorry, but we cannot make it any cheaper than this.
Unable to bear watching me make no progress at all on my thesis, a friend gave me some advice.
My son could not bear the pressure of the entrance exams and fell ill.
Unable to wait for his daughter to come home with his first grandchild, the father went to meet them in front of the station.
"We sincerely apologize. We are unable to meet your request."
There was so little information that the situation at the scene was impossible to make out.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to refuse/decline politely while saving face.
Often used with verbs of perception/decision:判断する,了承する,承認する,受け入れる,対応する,許可する.
Keigo form: ～いたし かねます (very polite); neutral: ～し かねる .
When giving a reason, it is often combined with ため,都合上,規定により,個人情報につきましては…
If you want to be direct/objective: use できない; if something is merely hard to do: ～にくい／づらい.

• Expresses “cannot/can hardly do” for reasons of circumstances, rules, ethics, authority, or insufficient information.
• Soft nuance that avoids saying “できない” directly; more polite, especially in refusals.
• It does not negate ability. Instead of “don't know how to do it”, it means “it is not convenient/not appropriate/not permitted to do it”.
• The form しかねます is keigo used when dealing with customers/business partners.
fields.notes:
• Common polite phrases: お受けしかねます／ご対応いたしかねます／ご希望に添いかねます。
• The progressive form expresses hesitation: 決めかねている, 断りかねて（hesitating to refuse）.
• Within a company/organization it is often used to avoid taking direct responsibility: 「弊社といたしましては…いたしかねます」。 explain: The sentence pattern is affirmative in form but negative in meaning.
You want to do something but cannot; doing something is difficult.
Formal sentence. Stiff style. ⏐ examples: 1. 申し訳ありませんが、私にはわかりかねます。
I'm sorry, but it is hard for me to understand.
2. そのようなご依頼は、お引き受けしかねます。
We can hardly accept a request like that.
mistakes: Using ～かねる to mean “not capable”: incorrect. It is a refusal based on one's position, not on ability.
Confusing it with ～かねない (risk): completely different meaning and direction.
Using ～しかねます in casual speech sounds stiff; use できない/むずかしいです in everyday conversation.
Leaving out the accompanying reason/circumstances makes the sentence sound abrupt: give the reason with ので／ため／都合上…

fields.connection: V (plain form) + かのようだ かのような N かのように / N (である)
examples: She began explaining as if she knew everything.
He was behaving as if nothing had happened.
fields.explain: ◎ Expresses that something looks or feels that way even though in reality it is not so. Often used with adverbs such as 「まるで」「いかにも」and「あたかも」.

examples: She's rich, and even her belongings are different from ours.
That kid is defiant, starting with the way they talk.
"Your argument is wrong right from its premise."
That hotel was luxurious, starting with its marble lobby.
This shop feels upscale from its atmosphere alone.
He is sloppy, starting with the way he dresses.
fields.explain:
Takes N as a “clue” and then gives an intuitive conclusion/evaluation.
Often used with negative words:変だ／怪しい／無理がある／失礼だ／安っぽい など。
Not used for clear objective causes; it leans toward subjective impressions.
Position: usually at the start of the clause or before the judgment: Nからして、～。

• A judgment based on a small sign: “Just looking at/judging only from N, you can tell…”. Example: 見た目からして高そうだ。
• Gives a typical example, “right from/even N…”, often implying something negative or unusual: 彼は挨拶からしてできていない。
• Emphasizes the “starting point” to infer the whole: a small part already shows the big picture.
• Nuance: subjective and more intuitive than からすると; often used to criticize, complain, or doubt whether something is right.
fields.notes:
• Often seen in spoken language, reviews and criticism because of its strong evaluative nuance.
• When N is something “overall” (雰囲気, 見た目, タイトル, 値段), からして is more natural.
• If you need to emphasize “even N…”, you can use: Nからして～ない／違う。
mistakes: Using it for an objective cause → Incorrect. Use ので／ため／ことから instead.
Attaching it to a verb clause → Incorrect. からして mainly attaches to nouns.
Confusing it with からすると: JLPT questions often test the nuance “negative vs neutral”.
Using it for excessive praise → Unnatural. からして usually leans negative or conveys a strong impression.

examples: Judging from this name, this person is probably Japanese.
From his point of view, they are probably all questions that are too easy.
Judging from these footprints, it's a bear, not a deer.
Judging from the symptoms, it is very likely influenza.
Given his personality, he wouldn't tell a lie like that.
From a parent's point of view, a child's safety comes first.
fields.explain:
Takes N as the basis and then makes an inference; often used in reports, analyses and news.
When it indicates a “standpoint”, the subject is usually a person/group:学生からすると／経営者からすると.
Moderate certainty; the conclusion often comes with an adverb/conjecture ending.
More formal than からして when used in logical reasoning.

• Inference: “Based on N, one can infer…”. Example: 症状からすると風邪だろう。
• Standpoint/viewpoint: “Seen from N's side…”. Example: 消費者からすると値上げは痛い。
• Neutral nuance, more rational than からして; can be used for both positive and negative conclusions.
• Often accompanied by uncertain judgments: ～だろう／～と思われる／～ようだ。
fields.notes:
• In written language, からすると suits conclusion clauses with a clear basis (データ、症状、状況、結果).
• からすれば sometimes implies “speaking from that position…”, with a more subjective nuance than からすると.
• With “people/groups”, both からすると and からすれば are natural: 消費者／親／専門家 など.
mistakes: Taking it as a direct cause → Incorrect. It is a basis for inference, not an actual reason.
Concluding too definitely (断定) → Unnatural. Use ～だろう／～と思われる.
Confusing it with からして in nuance questions: the JLPT often tests “negative impression” vs “neutral inference”.

examples: Just because something is expensive doesn't mean its quality is good.
Just because people are Japanese doesn't mean they all like sushi.
Not getting in touch just because you're busy is rude.
You shouldn't stop exercising just because it's cold.
Just because someone is a child doesn't mean they'll be forgiven no matter what they do.
Don't go buying things in bulk thoughtlessly just because they're cheap.
fields.explain:
The first clause states a “seemingly sufficient reason”, and the second clause negates or adjusts the expectation.
Common in debates, education, and rules of conduct.
In spoken language からって is used; in written, formal language からといって is used.
It usually avoids a strongly affirmative conclusion that accepts that reason.

• “Just because… (not necessarily/shouldn't)…”: negates mechanical thinking based on the preceding reason.
• Often combined with partial negation expressions: ～とは限らない／わけではない／とは言えない.
• Also used to warn about or criticize behavior based on an inadequate reason.
• Nuance: challenging prejudices, advising moderation and not making excuses.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～から.
→ ～からといって means “just because…, you cannot conclude/act that way”; it negates a simplistic inference.
2) The second clause is usually a negation or a reminder/advice.
→ Common forms: ～からといって、…とは限らない／…わけではない.
3) Not used to state a direct reason.
→ If you are just stating an ordinary cause, use ～から／～ので.
meaning_vi: Means “just because of the reason ~”
examples: 1. ①　治ったからって
Just because you've recovered from the illness.
2. ②　好きじゃないからといって、野菜を食べないのは体に悪い。
Not eating vegetables just because you don't like them is bad for your health.
3. ➂　バスケットボールの選手だからって、背が高いわけではない。
Just because someone is a basketball player doesn't mean they are tall. meaning_vi: Just because of the reason　～, ～ ⏐ explain: Just because of a reason, however, even so, not necessarily (you cannot draw a conclusion or assert something based on that one reason alone)
「～からって」 is used in spoken language ⏐ examples: 1. 好きだからといって、同じ食品ばかり食べるのはよくない。
It's not good to eat only the same food just because you like it.
2. 日本に住んでいるからといって、日本語がしゃべれるようにはならない。
Just because you live in Japan doesn't mean you will become able to speak Japanese.
mistakes: Second clause is a strong affirmative “should/is allowed” → Usually unnatural. This pattern leans toward negation/dissuasion.
Confusing it with といっても (lowering the degree) → The JLPT often sets traps with this pair.
Using the polite form (です/ます) directly in the first clause → Not grammatically wrong, but the JLPT favors the plain form.
Missing the negation/adjustment in the second clause → The meaning of the pattern is easily lost.

examples: Once you've made a promise, you must keep it without fail.
Since I'm taking part in the match, I intend to give it my all.
Since I'm going to study abroad, I want to achieve solid results.
As a professional, you have to prove yourself through results.
Now that we've come this far, there's no turning back.
Since they're taking the exam, they should pass / they're sure to pass.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a “commitment” or a “norm” after a prerequisite has happened or will happen.
The second clause often goes with: ～べきだ／～つもりだ／～てみせる／～ないわけにはいかない／～はずだ／～に違いない。
More formal than ～以上(は), ～上(は) in some contexts, but all three express “once…”.
V-たからには emphasizes that something has already happened; V-るからには can express determination before doing it.

• “Once…, then…”: states a strong premise that entails an obligation/determination/logical result.
• Two main nuances:

Obligation/determination (the speaker states/proposes a norm): やるからには最後までやり抜く。
Inevitable conjecture: 日本に来たからには、日本語はできるはずだ。

• Obligation/determination (the speaker states/proposes a norm): やるからには最後までやり抜く。
• Inevitable conjecture: 日本に来たからには、日本語はできるはずだ。
• The second clause usually contains a strong will/rule/expectation, not simply a statement of fact.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～以上（は）／～から.
→ ～からには means “once…, then…”; the second clause is usually an obligation/volition/determination.
2) The second clause usually has a nuance of obligation or responsibility.
→ If the second clause is just an ordinary description, this pattern usually does not fit.
3) Not used for light conditions.
→ For an ordinary “because/since”, use ～から／～ので.
mistakes: Second clause just states a fact → The nuance of obligation/determination is lost (misuse of the pattern).
Confusing it with からといって in sentences that negate a prejudice → Different function.
Missing a suitable option for the second clause (choosing an answer with no volition/norm) → A common N2 trap.
Using it with adjectives/nouns without である in formal writing → Unnatural/not standard.

examples: From an expert's point of view, this plan has a lot of problems.
Judging from the data, the economy is gradually recovering.
Through a child's eyes, the adult world is a strange place.
From a safety standpoint as well, repairing this bridge is an urgent task.
From a third party's standpoint, there are misunderstandings on both sides.
Judging from the satellite photos, the damage is greater than expected.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to make clear the “focus of the assessment” before stating a conclusion.
Suitable for both written and spoken language; moderately formal.
Not used to express benefit/relationship, i.e. personal feelings “for (someone)…” → prefer 〜にとって.
To emphasize conjecture, use 〜からすると; to emphasize the aspect/criterion of the statement, use 〜から言うと.
The conclusion after ～から見ると is usually a judgment, evaluation or inference, not a direct command.

～から見ると: “Seen from/if we consider (perspective/criterion/source of information)…, then…”. Expresses a judgment/comment based on a specific viewpoint or data.
• The focus is on the viewpoint/observation (visual/metaphorical). “見る” suggests a sense based on something that can be observed or interpreted.
• Often used with N indicating a source: データ・統計・専門家・第三者・子どもの目・外部・安全面・コスト面…
• Expresses relative objectivity; however, it is still the speaker's assessment based on the stated viewpoint.
• Variants: 見れば (supposition), 見ても (emphasizing “even considered from that…”).
fields.notes:
• N is usually a specific “eye/standpoint”: 研究者・医者・利用者・会計の面・文化の視点.
• With N referring to things/data sources (地図・統計・記録), the nuance is “observing from the data”.
• Avoid overusing it with commands/volition; switching to ので/から is more natural. | Variants: ～から見れば・から見て(も)
mistakes: Confusing it with 〜によれば/によると (reported source of information). から見ると is a judgment from a viewpoint, not “according to the forecast…”.
Using it for “for (someone)” (feelings) → incorrect. Correct form: 〜にとって.
Attaching it directly to a command: “専門家から見ると、やめろ” → crude; switch to an indirect recommendation.
JLPT: easily confused with からすると/から言うと. Look at the core verb: 見る=observation, 言う=statement/criterion, する=arriving at a conjecture.

Emphasizes the criterion for the statement/evaluation

fields.meaning: In terms of…, from the standpoint of…
examples: In terms of price, this model is the best deal.
In terms of quality, domestic products are more reassuring.
From a legal standpoint, that act is illegal.
From a grammatical point of view, this expression is unnatural.
Speaking from experience, the earlier you prepare, the better.
From the company's standpoint, a price increase is unavoidable.
fields.explain:
Used when you want to “set a framework of criteria” before making a judgment.
Suitable for written language, speeches and reports; natural in the context of debate.
Do not confuse it with the meaning “say that” of言う; here it marks a criterion.
Often used with phrases like の点から言うと/見地から言うと to make it sound more standard.

～から言うと: “In terms of/as regards/if we talk about (criterion)…, then…”. Used when setting an evaluation criterion and then giving an assessment.
• N is usually a criterion: 値段・品質・安全・法律・文法・効率・デザイン・立場 等.
• Its nuance is more reasoned/normative than 〜から見ると; less intuitive.
• The variants から言えば/から言って change the rhythm of the sentence and the level of formality.
fields.notes:
• “経験から言って” is a very natural phrase, almost fixed in advice.
• In academic fields: 歴史学から言うと／統計学の観点から言うと make it more convincing.
• In presentations, several criteria are combined in parallel: 価格・性能・デザインの点から言うと、Aが最適だ。 | Variants: ～から言えば・から言って
mistakes: Confusing it with “Aと言うと” (when it comes to A). 〜から言うと means “in terms of…”, not “speaking of…”.
Using から言うと for the subject's feelings “for (someone)” → incorrect. You must use 〜にとって.
Combining it with a direct command sounds harsh; use a recommendation/evaluation instead of giving an order.
JLPT: distinguish から見ると/からすると/から言うと by the core verb (見る/する/言う).

rows: <ruby>効率<rt>こうりつ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うと、Bが<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>い。
Seen from the perspective of N
<ruby>外部<rt>がいぶ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ると、<ruby>複雑<rt>ふくざつ</rt></ruby>だ。

Introduces a topic, not just a criterion
